subject: voxelWhale
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: humpback whale.
Style: voxel.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a voxel-style humpback whale built with the SDK, thinking through using blocky box shapes for texture and constructing the body as a chain of joints along the spine to keep the creature skeleton-first.

I'm sizing the whale at a realistic ~14 meters, with the body resting so its lowest point sits at floor level like it's floating, and figuring out the head-to-tail placement, body radius, and center height for a swimming pose with a slight tail curve. I'm working out the voxel unit size for the box-based construction.

I'm sizing paint texel density against cell size to make sure cellPaint resolution matches the voxel scale, landing on a 2048 paint canvas. Then I'm tallying up the part count: roughly 26 body slices plus extra details like head tubercles, barnacles, ventral pleat grooves, eyes, mouth line, and a separate lower jaw piece.

I'm planning the remaining pieces -- long flippers with leading-edge bumps, a notched fluke, small dorsal hump, and blowhole -- while deciding to skip extras like a blow spout or remoras since nothing beyond the whale itself was requested. For textures I'm settling on a handful of pixel-art textures (eye, fluke underside marking, ventral pleat pattern) to stay within the target range of 180-340 parts and 5-12 textures.

Now I'm narrowing the texture set to about six: eye, pleats, fluke-under pattern, barnacle speckles for chin/flipper edges, baleen stripes, and a scar tile, applying flat materials to boxes with cellPaint for the main body shading before moving on to defining the spine joint chain from head to tail.

I'm working out the body's rest pose — the centerline curve rising toward the tail, positioning the belly so it touches y=0 while the chest center sits around y=1.75, and checking that the downward-angled pectoral fins don't dip below the ground when extended. Now I'm starting to lay out the spine joints as a chain of named points running from head to tail.

Still defining the spine chain...

For the jaw, I'll hinge it near the rear of the mouth around z=4.4, parented to the head and aimed forward. For the tail, I'm chaining from the hips backward through points at z=-2.5, -5, -7, and -8.6, using names tail1 through tail4 plus a terminal "fluke" joint.

I want the tail to rise slightly along this chain for a natural resting pose, with y-values stepping up gradually—keeping boxes axis-aligned in the voxel style while letting the stair-step rise feel consistent with that aesthetic. I'm also considering how joint orientation works for chains without explicit orientation options, since bones might just default to world axes.

I'm building a helper function to generate box-shaped parts attached to bones, and mapping out which bone governs each z-range along the body—head, three spine segments, and four tail segments leading to the fluke tip. Now I'm sketching the body profile function, defining the half-width and vertical offsets at each z position to capture the humpback's broad, flat-rostrumed head shape.

I'm tabulating half-height and half-width values at various points along the body length, from the snout down through the tapering peduncle to the fluke root, making sure the tail stock comes out tall and laterally compressed rather than wide, matching real humpback anatomy.

Now I'm planning the slicing approach: dividing the body length into segments of fixed depth, snapping widths and heights to voxel-size multiples, and tracking the spine centerline so the slice tops and bottoms can be offset asymmetrically to capture the flatter head crown and the bulging lower jaw/belly.

Actually, maybe simpler to model it as three stacked boxes per slice: a dark central upper box, a dark flank lower box, and a white belly strip in between to capture the real humpback pattern of dark back, black flanks, and the pleated white throat-to-navel belly.

So the dark flank overhangs the white belly by one voxel, creating that stepped look with the white visible underneath near the throat. I'm varying belly height along the body—thicker near the throat for the pleats, thinner elsewhere, with the white fading out before the tail where the underside turns dark with a white patch. For the throat pleats themselves, I'm using a textured tile pattern to create grooved lines running along the body.

Working out tile sizing and texel density, then tackling an orientation problem: pleat lines need to run lengthwise along the body on both the bottom and side faces, but since the UV coordinates are mapped differently on each face, a tile that looks right on the bottom reads as the wrong direction on the sides. I'm considering whether a single tile could handle both orientations without turning into an unwanted checker pattern.

Still working out the pleat grid alignment...

That gives 28 slices totaling 15.68 m, fitting a humpback's typical 14-16 m length nicely, with snout at 6.72 and tail/fluke start at -8.96. I'm indexing the slices so centers sit at the midpoint of each 0.56 m band, then mapping cell coordinates on each face to grid-aligned u/v values based on the relevant axes.

I'm checking float precision at face boundaries—jitter only applies along the normal axis, keeping tangential positions interior and clean. For the dark body, I'm using smaller 0.14 cell sizes for mottling variety while keeping edges grid-aligned, pairing it with a dark navy-slate color ramp.

Lighting logic brightens the top using normal-based blending plus noise, mimicking a humpback's darker back, with occasional pale scar speckles added randomly. Since boxes share the same world-space paint pattern, the texture continues seamlessly across adjacent boxes—now I'm setting up the belly paint with alternating light/dark bands based on cell parity along different axes.

Now I'm adding random dark mottled patches to the belly for realism, plus small bump-like tubercle knobs along the rostrum and chin using tiny cubes to mimic the humpback's characteristic facial knobs.

I also want a mouth groove line along the head and a separate jointed lower jaw mesh, since humpback lower jaws protrude and rock on their own bone—splitting the head slices above z≈3.9 into upper head versus jaw sections so the jaw can move independently.

Still working out head geometry...

I realize the single-row check picks the band just below y_m, giving one 0.14-thick dark line for the jaw/mouth boundary, but this should only apply within the head region where ymouth is actually defined, returning null elsewhere. I also need to account for the mouth line continuing rearward toward the eye area where the humpback's mouth rises.

Checking consistency: I'm matching the jaw/head split height at each slice to the same ym(z) function so everything snaps together, keeping the mouth closed in the rest pose. For the eye, I'm placing a small pixel-art textured plane near the mouth corner on each side of the head, facing outward in the x direction.

I need a helper that computes slice parameters (center z, half-width, bottom/top y) so the eye can sit flush against the correct side face, quantized to that slice's width plus a small offset. For the eye texture itself, I'm sketching a simple 8x8 whale eye pattern with a dark pupil, lighter surround, and a white glint, using transparent pixels around it.

Above the eye I'll add a small brow ridge box, and for the blowhole I'm placing two thin dark slit boxes on top of the head near the back, plus small raised splashguard ridges around them.

Now I'm working out the pectoral flippers -- long appendages roughly a third of body length, attached at the chest below mid-height, built as a joint chain of three segments extending sideways and angled back from each shoulder.

Writing flipper box segments...

Working out the flipper geometry: chord profile tapering along the length, with the chord center shifting backward and the vertical position descending toward the tip to give a slight downward tilt. I'm making the top surface dark and the underside white and thicker, matching the mostly-white coloring typical of humpback flippers.

Adding leading-edge tubercle knobs (seven small bumps per fin along the front edge) and giving the trailing edge a wavy, irregular shape. I'm also assigning bone segments along the flipper boxes — shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand — and making sure the flipper root tucks into the body at the shoulder junction rather than floating outside it, adjusting the attachment height accordingly.

Checking that the fin tip stays above the belly line so nothing clips below y=0, then sketching out the joint path as a simple polyline through a few key points along the flipper's length rather than a smooth curve, since joint rotation doesn't matter much for rigid boxes. Now I'm moving on to designing the horizontal tail fluke.

I'm laying out the fluke as stepped boxes forming two swept-back triangular wings off a central root, with leading and trailing edges computed per column to create the tapering, notched shape with a serrated trailing edge.

Now I need to reconcile the fluke joint position with the tail chain endpoint, moving the path's last point to z=-8.96 to match where the tail slices begin, and work out the spine's y-position curve piecewise across different z ranges.

Then I'm snapping the slice centers and dimensions to grid multiples of V, so that heights and widths at each z-position quantize cleanly, keeping the lowest belly point consistent across the chain.

I'm sketching out numeric width and height profiles at various z-slices along the body to capture the taper from the snout back through the thickest section and down toward the tail, accounting for the lower jaw bulge and the dorsal hump near the fin.

I'm sketching out the mouth line position and adjusting the head's top profile to slope gently from front to back, tuning Hu and Hb values at each cross-section so the jaw and upper head curve smoothly toward the snout tip.

Continuing the slice centers, I settle the spine path at z-values 0, 1.5, 3.0, and 4.5, dividing it into spine1, spine2, and spine3 segments, with the head bone taking over past z=4.5 where the higher slices (zc 6.44, 5.88, 5...) belong.

Settling on 6 slices with head length at 21% of body, placing the eye and jaw split on the slice at zc=3.64, and positioning the pectoral fin behind at z≈1.9. I'm also defining the mouth rise with a conditional offset based on zc thresholds, then mapping out where ventral pleats run from chin to navel.

Now I'm working out the belly coloring—white extending to about z=-4 then turning dark, with a similar white patch on the tail underside and flukes. I'm placing the jaw hinge joint near the head tip, aiming it forward to the snout, and deciding how to structure the joint chain naming so the head joint sits correctly within the spine chain with the right parent-role relationships.

Still structuring the rig hierarchy—working out the spine chain with three spans and a separate head joint parented to spine3, placing the hips as the root joint with spine and tail chains branching off as children.

Now mapping z-coordinate ranges to specific bones for the spine chain, and extending that same slicing logic into the tail chain with four segments ending in a fluke tip.

Then I'm sketching the dorsal fin: a small stepped hump near the tail boundary topped with a backward-swept triangular fin, working out box dimensions for the hump's width, height, and length.

I'm also planning the tubercle knobs along the head and jaw, placing small random cubes on the top surface of the head slices to mimic the bumpy texture.

Then I'm adding a chin knob and pale barnacle clusters near the chin, flipper edges, and throat for extra surface detail.

Next I need a barnacle cluster texture for patches on the chin, jaw, and flipper edges, plus a fluke underside texture with a mottled black-and-white pattern. For the fluke undersides I'm thinking through how to avoid repeating the same tile pattern across columns, maybe using a noise-based approach so the pattern stays continuous rather than obviously tiled.

Deciding on the final texture set to use: eye, barnacle cluster, orca rake scars (parallel light lines on the flank), flipper underside markings (white with black speckled edges), and baleen — while handling softer patterns like the fluke underside coloring with cell noise rather than a texture map.

Switching strategy for the fluke: instead of stacked stair columns, I'll use an extrude shape with a stepped outline to get a voxel-style silhouette, then paint top vs bottom faces differently using the surface normal to tell top from bottom.

Settling on a texture set: EYE, BARN, RAKE, and a FLIP pattern for the flipper underside boxes, each with slightly different crops via randomized stepping, using pixelTexture and cellPaint for the patches.

I'll add small stair-step serrations along the dorsal ridge of the tail for that voxel edge look. Tallying up the part count across all the pieces—slices, flippers, knobs, fin, barnacles—I'm estimating somewhere around 150-200 total voxel parts for the whole model.

Now I'm working out additional surface details: ventral throat grooves done via paint rather than geometry, a darker tint on the lower jaw front, and a scattering of smaller tubercles along the jaw sides. With that settled, I'm starting to sketch out the actual builder API call and imports needed from the voxel kit library to construct this piece by piece.

Writing helper functions and types...

I'm thinking about how the box geometries get painted with per-vertex colors using UV charts, estimating how many slices and packed tiles the atlas needs, and roughly calculating texel density to make sure everything fits within a 2048 or 4096 texture size.

I'm thinking through whether I can safely strip hidden internal faces from each slice's box geometry to save area, but it's tricky since adjacent slices of different sizes expose step faces that need to stay visible. The real fix is only dropping a slice's end face when the neighboring cross-section fully covers it, otherwise keeping it.

For the belly, I'm setting up a cell-painting function with a 0.28 grid that produces alternating pleats/grooves on the bottom face, sharing one paint-sheet material across parts.

Now I'm adding speckled darker patches near the chin using noise-based variation, then defining a darker color ramp for the dark body paint...

Still refining the body shading...

Working through the belly's pleat beneath the jaw, then defining the per-slice parameters: computing z-center positions across the 28 slices from front to back, snapping the y-center to the grid, and deriving the half-width from the width function at each depth.

Still refining slice logic...

Now I'm working out the head slice offsets, mapping each z-coordinate band to its y-midpoint shift to model the jaw hinge transition around z=3.6-3.9, where the bone geometry closes toward the rear.

Checking the front slices though, I notice a conflict: the belly's bottom-plus-height calculation overshoots the jaw midpoint at zc=6.44, meaning I need to shrink the belly height for the frontmost slices to avoid the belly region overlapping past ym.

I'm adjusting jaw dark box logic so bh is clamped relative to (ym−yBot), skipping the dark jaw band entirely if the jaw region is too thin to render cleanly.

Now I'm adding a chin knob protrusion at the jaw tip, positioning it as a separate box slightly offset below the mouth line, and planning eye placement by computing which z-slice corresponds to the eye position and offsetting from the jaw's top surface at that slice.

Designing eye pixel art...

Placing the blowhole at the top of a slice near the head, with a splashguard rim made of side and rear ridge boxes, plus two dark slit boxes for the actual opening.

Now I'm working out the flipper geometry: for each side, a sequence of eight boxes stepping outward from the body root at x=1.4, each 0.56 wide, reaching a tip distance around 5.3-5.9 from center, extending well beyond the body's width at that z-position.

I'm also tapering the chord length along the flipper, sweeping the leading edge slightly inward with each segment, and dropping the vertical center position progressively outward to give the flipper a natural downward curve while making sure the lowest point still stays above zero.

Now I'm defining the thickness profile: a thicker dark top box tapering toward the tip and a thinner white underside box, both centered relative to each segment's vertical position, plus adding small leading-edge knobs along the flipper for texture.

For the flipper underside, I'm generating a tiled texture with a pale base color scattered with gray flecks to simulate a mottled surface, checking that the texture colors read as distinct enough to render properly when mapped onto the geometry.

For the flipper's top surface I'm using the body's paint ramp instead of a separate scheme, and mapping the flipper's box segments to the joint chain's shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand positions to drive its articulation.

Still working out joint spacing...

Mapping joints to box indices...

Still computing column geometry...

Working out the trailing edge extent, total fluke depth comes to about 1.9 meters rooted near z=-8.7. For each column I'm computing cell index ranges from the leading and trailing measurements divided by slice thickness, making sure adjacent columns overlap properly so the extrusion stays continuous.

Checking the central notch region where the chord narrows significantly—confirming cell counts still produce valid ranges there, and planning to add root columns so the tail stock tapers smoothly into the fluke. Settling on extrusion thickness around 0.2 with no bevel, and snapping the fluke's y-position to about 3.0 based on the computed curve value.

I'm verifying the extrusion axes cross correctly to give an upward-facing normal, then setting up the paint logic so top faces get a dark pattern, bottom faces get a white pattern, and side walls stay dark based on their normal direction.

Writing bottom pattern noise...

I'm placing the fluke joint at the tail root and defining a `stepped` helper that generates staircase outlines for a cell grid, checking that the sharp-point outline won't self-intersect when extruded.

For the tail peduncle, I'm adding small ridge boxes along the top of the last few tail slices, alternating placement and matching bone/color per slice, then locating the dorsal fin slice index near z≈-3.64.

The dorsal hump needs a base box spanning two adjacent slices, then a stacked set of thinner fin steps shrinking in width and height moving toward the tip, layered on top of the hump.

Now I'm thinking about rake scar textures — flat decal-like planes on the flanks with parallel diagonal lines, sized relative to the body's half-width at that z-position, computed via a helper function that looks up slice widths. I also want to add barnacle patches near the chin, head top, and flipper leading edges using thin planes.

Placing barnacle texture planes...

I'm placing side knobs on the jaw and a larger chin knob underneath, plus adding throat pleat grooves for texture. I'm also setting up the color palette constants and double-checking that the belly's lowest point aligns correctly with the snapped height table.

Checking the snapped height values confirms the body's bottom edge sits flush at y=0, touching the floor as intended. Now I'm estimating overall model height, factoring in the raised flukes, dorsal fin, and body curve to get a max height around 3.5 units.

Setting up tail joint positions by snapping y-values at each z-depth along the tail. Defining the spine chain with evenly spaced joints from the hips outward, naming them spine1 through spine3.

Now I'm attaching the flipper chains to spine2 near z≈2, with left/right naming based on sign of x, plus the jaw and head joints anchored to the spine with aim directions pointing forward.

The hips serve as the unparented root joint, with all other joints and chains specifying a parent explicitly. I'm starting to write out the actual TypeScript imports for the builder utilities and pixel-kit helpers needed for the rigging and painting code.

Now I'm defining size constants and an interpolation helper, then building a lookup table of body measurements (head width, body width, torso height) keyed by z-height, sorted from top to bottom.

I also need a function for computing the y-center offset at each height, plus a loop constructing slice objects with their centers, half-widths, top/bottom y-bounds, and bone assignments.

I'm defining the belly height logic based on z-position thresholds, and double-checking the slice thickness adds up correctly near the tail-head transition, while also making sure the minimum half-width doesn't collapse too small near the tail end.

Writing slice-building loop...

Still refining jaw geometry...

Checking jaw heights across other z-slices to confirm the belly dark band always stays at least one unit tall, down to the shortest jaw point where it reduces to the minimum.

Otherwise the whole segment stays dark. I need to handle the mouth line for body slices using the axis and position, checking that the jaw box's end face at the transition point matches the body slice's width so the seam looks continuous, then map head slices to the head bone, jaw slices to the jaw bone, and body slices to the body bone.

Now I'm defining a helper function to place boxes with a given size, position, color, bone, and extra options like texture. For the under-flipper tiles and barnacle patches, I'm writing helper functions that create textured plane geometries attached to bones, using an optional "up" parameter alongside a z-axis orientation to control how the patch leans.

I'm sketching out a pixel-art texture palette for the barnacle, with colors for white, gray, dark, and lice-orange, then drafting the row-by-row pixel grid for an 8x8 pattern.

Still designing the pixel grid...

Writing belly paint logic...

Fine letting the fluke paint fall back to the body paint, since nested paints resolve correctly through the cell grid. Now checking the jaw geometry details, like the inset width for the lower jaw's dark box faces.

Adding the ridge boxes on the tail dorsal, and the flukes underside is done. Keeping the pose straight rather than curving it.

Writing flipper placement code...

I'm verifying joint positions align with box centers correctly, checking the shoulder point lands inside the body mesh, and setting up the flipper chain with named joints for shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand.

Still writing box tiling loop...

Adding knob coloring, barnacle patches at the leading edge, and now working out the dorsal fin height using slice lookups near the body's midsection.

Still working out positioning...

Now placing the eyes symmetrically using the bone head, positioning them along the chin slice with calculated y-coordinates, and adding small eyebrow boxes above each. I'll finalize snapping all boxes into place, set the meta name to "Humpback Whale", and double-check the mouth line detail on the upper jaw box.

Then I'm verifying the body generation functions compile correctly—checking cell random/pick calls, noise function signature, and vector access patterns. I'm also confirming nothing dips below y=0 by tracing the belly, chin, fluke, and flipper positions, then checking the hips joint parameters.

Now I'm setting up the tail chain with four segments plus a fluke tip, mapping bone references for each spine and tail joint, and computing the fluke's extrusion position by snapping its y-coordinate to the nearest slice.

Working out span widths and chord lengths for each tail segment based on distance from center, with serrated adjustments on alternating columns...

Still computing span overlaps...

Outline point count is within budget. I'm defining a mouth-height function that steps between three y-levels depending on z-range, and checking whether the body paint condition for the mouth line correctly aligns with the voxel grid's cell centers near the z=4.5 boundary, since there could be a mismatch there.

Good, the edges land on multiples of 0.28 as expected. Now I'm checking the final details: knob positions, making sure the root export and bone/part references are typed correctly, adding texture generation with fill and fleck patterns, and confirming the barn's plane normals and side directions are set up right.

Now I'm placing the remaining patches — one near the rostrum oriented toward the head's up axis, and jaw side patches positioned along the dark region of the jaw box. I'm also tallying up the textures used (EYE, BARN_A, BARN_B, RAKE, FLIP) to confirm there are five, and considering whether to add a white flank spot texture before finalizing the code.

Setting up the module structure now: defining the build function that creates the humpback whale builder, keeping paint and texture generation inside the build function for determinism rather than at module level. I'm writing a profile interpolation helper that looks up body measurements at a given z-coordinate by walking through a table of control points and linearly blending between them.

Adding head tubercle knobs...

Finishing writing the code carefully...
